title: Internal Currency: The Corporate Token Economy
body:
Every major corporation in GLMZ operates its own internal currency system alongside the Meridian Quantum Credit standard. These systems go by various names — Helion Dynamics uses 'Flux Credits,' the Nakamura-Osei Group uses 'Merit Tokens,' and the smaller but influential Verdana BioSystems uses 'Growth Points' — but they share a common architecture: they are earned through performance and loyalty behaviors, they are redeemable only within the corporation's ecosystem, they expire on a rolling schedule that typically ranges from ninety days to one year, and they cannot be converted to external currency. This last feature is not incidental. It is the foundational design principle that makes the system function as a retention mechanism rather than a compensation supplement.

The earning mechanics of internal currency are calibrated to reinforce the behavioral patterns corporations most want to encourage. Attending optional training sessions, submitting innovation proposals through internal channels, achieving high alignment fidelity scores in review cycles, participating in corporate social initiatives, and maintaining social network connections that are deemed 'brand-positive' all generate token accrual. Conversely, filing a formal HR complaint, accessing external legal resources, or registering with any of the recognized labor advocacy organizations automatically triggers a token freeze period of thirty to sixty days — technically described in policy documents as an 'administrative hold during dispute resolution.' The chilling effect on employees considering whether to raise workplace concerns is well-documented.

The redemption ecosystem for internal currency is extensive and deliberately designed to be genuinely useful. In a typical Tier-1 corporate zone, tokens can be applied to housing tier upgrades, healthcare access expansions, educational credits for dependents, premium transit access, restaurant and retail purchases within the zone's commercial district, and what corporations call 'experience allocations' — access to recreational facilities, cultural events, and off-zone excursions organized and supervised by the corporation. The system is sophisticated enough that many employees structure their discretionary spending entirely around token accumulation strategies, treating the internal economy as their primary financial planning framework rather than their Quantum Credit salary. This is precisely the intended outcome: it deepens the employee's material dependence on continued corporate employment beyond what salary alone would create.

Financial analysts who cover corporate sector dynamics for Meridian's independent investment platforms have noted that internal currency systems function as a form of off-balance-sheet compensation liability management. Because tokens expire and cannot be converted, corporations can offer what appears to be generous total compensation while retaining the ability to effectively claw back a significant portion of that compensation through expiration if an employee leaves or is terminated before redeeming accrued tokens. The legal status of accrued but unredeemed tokens in separation agreements is the subject of ongoing litigation. The Meridian Commercial Court has issued contradictory rulings in different cases depending on how the specific token system was classified in the employment contract — as compensation, as benefit, or as a discretionary corporate program — and no unified standard has emerged.
